description: We are Year 2 University Students. We are enthusiastic about space game missions.
summary:
Space Bar is an interactive, bilingual space-mission simulator designed to help students understand how real missions are engineered and flown. Players build rockets piece by piece, compare authentic spacecraft, manage mass, fuel, power, payload, and budget, then guide their vehicle through launch, staging, atmospheric drag, gravity turns, orbital insertion, docking, satellite deployment, and planetary exploration.

The updated Guided Orbit Mission gives students a clear starting point: configure a Saturn V payload, examine how engineering choices affect cost, thrust-to-weight ratio, and performance, and fly a physics-based ascent with optional guidance. Live telemetry, educational explanations, historical missions, post-flight feedback, an encyclopedia, and English/French accessibility turn complex concepts into an engaging learning experience.

Space Bar addresses the challenge by connecting mission planning, spacecraft design, resource trade-offs, and flight operations within one interactive system. It is important because students do not simply read about spaceflight—they experiment, encounter consequences, learn from failure, and discover why successful exploration depends on both scientific ambition and careful engineering.
details:
Project Details

Space Bar is an interactive educational spaceflight simulator in which students design, build, manage, and fly complete space missions. Players assemble rockets piece by piece, attach components vertically or laterally, choose payloads, build satellites and rovers, and monitor engineering constraints such as budget, mass, thrust-to-weight ratio, fuel, power, drag, and structural limits.

The Guided Orbit Mission provides an accessible starting point. Students configure a Saturn V payload and then follow a realistic ascent involving liftoff, a gravity turn, Max-Q, staging, coasting, and orbital insertion. Live telemetry shows altitude, velocity, fuel, drag, apoapsis, and periapsis, while contextual explanations describe why events occur. More experienced players can explore the complete construction sandbox, manual flight controls, docking, historical campaigns, spacecraft comparisons, mission data, achievements, and scientific exploration. English and French interfaces, light and dark themes, adjustable assistance, and learning feedback make the experience accessible to a wider range of students.

We developed the project using TypeScript, HTML, CSS, Vite, Three.js, and Vitest. The simulation uses SI units and models thrust, changing vehicle mass, atmospheric density, aerodynamic drag, gravity, staging, and orbital motion. A structured spacecraft and parts database connects vehicle appearance, dimensions, cost, and performance to the simulation.

The project is creative because it combines a construction game, physics simulator, mission-management experience, historical campaign, and educational tool in one system. Instead of presenting space science as isolated facts, it lets students experiment with connected decisions and immediately observe their consequences.

Our team considered scientific accuracy, student comprehension, accessibility, limited classroom time, performance on common computers, realistic spacecraft proportions, intuitive controls, and the importance of learning through both success and failure. The intended impact is to make aerospace engineering approachable and inspire students to explore science, technology, engineering, and mathematics through active problem-solving.
